analysis.one_liner: Lets commercial and rental real estate owners write off buildings over 20 years instead of decades, with inflation-proofed deductions.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would speed up tax write-offs for commercial and rental property owners, never got a hearing or a vote and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current tax law, owners of office buildings, stores, and rental apartments recover their costs slowly — over 39 years for commercial property and 27.5 years for rentals. This bill would cut that to 20 years and would also inflate each year's deduction, plus add a 3%-a-year growth factor, so owners could deduct more than they actually paid, in today's dollars, over the life of the building. That means faster, bigger tax savings for real estate investors, and less federal revenue. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, got 13 Republican cosponsors, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners and investors in commercial buildings and rental housing — including real estate partnerships, S corporations, and REITs, which the bill text specifically names — would gain the most, because faster and inflation-indexed depreciation means bigger tax deductions early in a building's life. Because these deductions are worth most to investors in high tax brackets, the benefit concentrates among wealthier real estate owners.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Commercial and rental real estate investors

how_it_helps.text: The bill classifies nonresidential real property and residential rental property as 20-year property for depreciation, replacing the current 39-year and 27.5-year recovery periods [S2] [S3].

It adds a 'neutral cost recovery' adjustment that multiplies each year's deduction by an inflation index and a 3% annual growth factor, increasing the total real value of deductions owners can claim [S3].

The bill explicitly extends the new deduction rules through pass-through entities — partnerships, S corporations, estates, trusts, and REITs — the structures most real estate investment flows through [S3].

Supporters' stated rationale, reflected in the bill's title, is that faster cost recovery encourages investment in buildings and supply-chain facilities; shorter recovery periods do reduce the tax penalty on new construction relative to current law.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, through reduced federal revenue: every deduction real estate owners claim is revenue the Treasury does not collect, which must be made up through other taxes, higher borrowing, or less spending. Because the benefit goes mainly to higher-income property investors, the net effect shifts tax burden away from that group toward everyone else.

drawbacks.text: The 3% real-growth multiplier means owners can deduct more, in real terms, than the building actually cost — a subsidy beyond simple cost recovery, financed by other taxpayers [S3].

The benefits flow overwhelmingly through real estate partnerships, S corporations, and REITs, whose owners skew toward higher incomes, so the tax savings concentrate at the top while the revenue loss is shared broadly [S3].
A faster write-off rewards buying existing buildings just as much as building new ones, so there is no guarantee of the new construction or supply-chain investment the bill's title promises.

An honest supporter would concede that the bill removes real property from eligibility for current-law bonus depreciation, a partial offset, but the net effect still front-loads and enlarges deductions for property owners [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The policy argument for faster depreciation — that 39-year schedules overstate real income because they ignore inflation — has real merit, and the bill's indexing attempt addresses it. But the 3% growth multiplier goes beyond fixing that problem, handing owners deductions larger than their actual cost, and the bill is narrowly targeted at one asset class held disproportionately by the wealthy. Whatever investment benefit might trickle out, the direct effect is a large, permanent tax preference for real estate investors paid for by the general taxpayer. As drafted, the costs outweigh the public benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from introduction in March 2022 until the Congress ended in January 2023, with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Jackie Walorski (R-IN) introduced the bill on March 24, 2022, with 10 original Republican cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee [S1] [S3] [S5].
It attracted 13 Republican cosponsors in total and no Democratic support [S4].
After Rep. Walorski's death in August 2022, Rep. Kevin Hern (R-OK) took over first sponsorship of the bill in November 2022 so cosponsors could continue to be added [S5].
The Ways and Means Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Real estate investors are no better off — the tax break never advanced — while federal taxpayers avoided a revenue loss that would have flowed mainly to high-income property owners.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers, who avoided the revenue loss

industries.industry: Commercial real estate owners and investors
industries.note: The bill would cut the commercial depreciation period from 39 years to 20 and inflate the deductions, sharply raising after-tax returns on office, retail, and industrial property. The revenue cost falls on all taxpayers while the benefit concentrates among property owners, who skew wealthy.

A 20-year recovery period and indexed deductions would raise after-tax returns on apartment buildings. Landlords argue faster write-offs support new housing supply, but the same write-off applies to purchases of existing buildings, and nothing in the bill conditions the benefit on building new units or lowering rents.

industries.industry: Real estate investment trusts (REITs) and pass-through partnerships
industries.note: The bill's new deduction rules explicitly reach REITs, partnerships, and S corporations, the main vehicles for large-scale real estate investment, enlarging their deductions without any new obligation toward tenants or the public.
Every dollar of faster or enlarged depreciation is federal revenue forgone, which must be offset through other taxes, borrowing, or spending cuts that land on the broad public.
